pages.question: A 62-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for a routine annual physical examination. He has a history of well-controlled hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus, managed with oral medications. He reports no current symptoms, including no flank pain, hematuria, or changes in urinary habits. As part of the evaluation, an abdominal ultrasound is performed, which reveals a 3 cm solitary, thin-walled, anechoic cyst on the superior pole of the left kidney with posterior acoustic enhancement and no internal septations, calcifications, or solid components. The remainder of the kidneys appear normal, with no evidence of hydronephrosis or other masses. What is the most appropriate management for this finding?

answers.text: Contrast-enhanced CT scan for further characterization

pages.question: A 62-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for a routine annual physical examination. He has a history of well-controlled hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus, managed with oral medications. He reports no current symptoms, including no flank pain, hematuria, or changes in urinary habits. As part of the evaluation, an abdominal ultrasound is performed, which reveals a 3 cm solitary, thin-walled, anechoic cyst on the superior pole of the left kidney with posterior acoustic enhancement and no internal septations, calcifications, or solid components. The remainder of the kidneys appear normal, with no evidence of hydronephrosis or other masses. What is the most appropriate management for this finding?

answers.text:
Contrast-enhanced CT scan for further characterization
(3.08%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The ultrasound demonstrates a simple renal cyst (Bosniak category I) based on its anechoic appearance, thin wall, posterior acoustic enhancement, and absence of septations, calcifications, or solid components. Simple cysts are benign and require no further evaluation or follow-up. Features concerning for malignancy include thick or irregular walls, septations, calcifications, solid components, or enhancement on contrast imaging - none of which are present in this case.
(Choice A)
Surgical excision of the cyst
Surgical excision is not indicated for asymptomatic simple renal cysts, which are benign lesions. Surgery would only be considered for symptomatic cysts causing pain, infection, or urinary obstruction, or for suspicious masses concerning for malignancy.
(Choice B)
Reassurance and no further follow-up
This is the correct management for a simple renal cyst, which is benign and asymptomatic, requiring no additional evaluation.
(Choice C)
Contrast-enhanced CT scan for further characterization
Contrast-enhanced CT is unnecessary for simple cysts that have classic benign features on ultrasound (anechoic, thin-walled, posterior acoustic enhancement, no septations or solid components). CT with contrast would be indicated if the ultrasound showed complex features requiring Bosniak classification.
(Choice D)
Serial ultrasound surveillance every 6 months
Serial imaging surveillance is not required for simple renal cysts, which have a benign natural history. Follow-up imaging would be appropriate for Bosniak category IIF (indeterminate) cysts or if the initial imaging showed any complex features requiring monitoring.
(Choice E)
Fine-needle aspiration biopsy
Fine-needle aspiration is not indicated for simple renal cysts as they are benign lesions with characteristic imaging features. Biopsy is reserved for complex or suspicious masses with concerning features such as thick walls, septations, or solid components that suggest malignancy.

pages.question: A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of persistent dry cough and intermittent wheezing. She reports that symptoms began shortly after an episode at a family gathering where she choked on a small olive pit while eating. She coughed vigorously at the time but felt better initially. On examination, vital signs are normal, and lung auscultation reveals decreased breath sounds and wheezing over the right lower lung field. A chest x-ray is obtained. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has persistent cough and unilateral wheezing after a choking episode on an olive pit, suggestive of foreign body aspiration. Chest x-ray is normal, which occurs in approximately 30% of foreign body aspiration cases, particularly with radiolucent organic materials. Bronchoscopy is the procedure of choice for both diagnosis and therapeutic removal when clinical suspicion is high.
(Choice A)
Bronchoscopy
Bronchoscopy is the most appropriate next step for definitive diagnosis and removal of a suspected aspirated foreign body, especially when clinical suspicion is high despite a normal x-ray.
(Choice B)
Empiric antibiotics
Antibiotics treat bacterial infections but do not address the mechanical obstruction from an aspirated foreign body. While post-obstructive pneumonia can occur as a complication of retained foreign bodies, the acute presentation with clear temporal relationship to choking indicates mechanical obstruction as the primary problem requiring removal.
(Choice C)
Computed tomography of the chest
While CT chest provides more detailed imaging and could potentially identify radiolucent foreign bodies, it delays definitive management. In cases with high clinical suspicion of foreign body aspiration, bronchoscopy offers both diagnostic and therapeutic capabilities in a single procedure, making it the preferred initial approach.
(Choice D)
Repeat chest x-ray in 24 hours
Chest X-rays are normal in approximately 30% of foreign body aspiration cases, particularly with radiolucent objects like organic materials. Waiting 24 hours risks complications such as post-obstructive pneumonia, atelectasis, or further migration of the foreign body.
(Choice E)
Observation and reassurance
Observation is inappropriate given the history of choking and persistent symptoms, as untreated foreign body aspiration can lead to complications like infection or atelectasis.

pages.question: A 65-year-old man with a history of depression presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe pain in his left eye, blurred vision, headache, and nausea that began 3 hours ago, shortly after he started a new prescription for amitriptyline. He reports seeing halos around lights. On examination, the left eye shows conjunctival injection, corneal edema, a shallow anterior chamber, and a mid-dilated, unreactive pupil. Intraocular pressure is 55 mm Hg in the left eye and 18 mm Hg in the right eye. What is the most appropriate initial management?

answers.text:
Discontinue amitriptyline and monitor intraocular pressure
(19.74%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has acute angle-closure glaucoma precipitated by the anticholinergic effects of amitriptyline, presenting with eye pain, blurred vision, headache, nausea, halos, and elevated intraocular pressure. Initial management focuses on rapidly reducing intraocular pressure with systemic acetazolamide and topical agents like beta-blockers, followed by definitive laser iridotomy. Discontinuing the medication alone is insufficient acutely. Immediate laser iridotomy is not initial; medical therapy is first. Corticosteroids and antivirals are not indicated for this condition.
(Choice A)
Discontinue amitriptyline and monitor intraocular pressure
While discontinuing the precipitating anticholinergic medication (amitriptyline) is important to prevent further pupillary dilation and angle closure, this alone is insufficient as initial management. The acute elevation in intraocular pressure (55 mmHg) requires immediate pharmacologic intervention to prevent irreversible optic nerve damage.
(Choice B)
Oral acyclovir
Oral acyclovir is used for viral infections such as herpes zoster ophthalmicus, which can present with severe eye pain and headache. However, viral conditions do not cause the characteristic findings of acute angle-closure glaucoma: elevated intraocular pressure (55 mmHg), shallow anterior chamber, and mid-dilated unreactive pupil.
(Choice C)
Immediate laser iridotomy
While laser peripheral iridotomy is the definitive treatment for acute angle-closure glaucoma, it should not be performed immediately. Initial medical therapy is needed first to lower intraocular pressure and reduce corneal edema, which will improve visualization and make the laser procedure safer and more effective.
(Choice D)
Intravenous acetazolamide and topical timolol
This combination rapidly lowers intraocular pressure by reducing aqueous humor production (acetazolamide) and outflow resistance (timolol), serving as appropriate initial therapy before definitive laser iridotomy.
(Choice E)
Topical corticosteroids
Topical corticosteroids are indicated for inflammatory eye conditions such as anterior uveitis but have no role in acute angle-closure glaucoma. In fact, steroids could potentially worsen intraocular pressure in some patients and would not address the underlying mechanical obstruction of aqueous outflow.

pages.question: A 28-year-old graphic designer presents to her primary care physician complaining of ongoing mood fluctuations that have affected her work and relationships for the past 4 years. She describes periods lasting several days to weeks where she feels unusually energetic, creative, and requires less sleep, during which she takes on multiple projects but often doesn't complete them. These alternate with periods of feeling mildly down, unmotivated, and socially withdrawn, though she can still function at her job. She denies any history of severe depressive episodes with suicidal ideation, significant weight changes, or inability to work, and has never experienced full manic symptoms like grandiosity, reckless behavior, or psychosis. Her symptoms have never fully remitted for more than 2 months at a time. She has no history of substance use or medical conditions. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient's chronic, fluctuating mood disturbance over 4 years, with subthreshold hypomanic and depressive symptoms that alternate without meeting full criteria for major depressive, hypomanic, or manic episodes, is consistent with cyclothymic disorder. The diagnosis requires at least 2 years of such symptoms with no symptom-free periods longer than 2 months, distinguishing it from other bipolar spectrum disorders that require discrete episodes meeting full diagnostic criteria.
(Choice A)
Major depressive disorder
Major depressive disorder requires at least one major depressive episode lasting at least 2 weeks with five or more symptoms (depressed mood, anhedonia, weight changes, sleep disturbance, fatigue, worthlessness/guilt, concentration problems, psychomotor changes, or suicidal ideation) causing significant functional impairment. This patient's depressive symptoms are mild, chronic, and do not cause significant impairment or meet the full symptom criteria.
(Choice B)
Borderline personality disorder
Borderline personality disorder features unstable relationships, self-image, and affects, with impulsivity and fear of abandonment. While mood instability can occur, this patient's symptoms are more consistent with a primary mood disorder without the interpersonal and self-harm features typical of borderline personality disorder.
(Choice C)
Cyclothymic disorder
Cyclothymic disorder is characterized by at least 2 years of numerous periods with hypomanic symptoms and depressive symptoms that do not meet criteria for hypomanic/manic or major depressive episodes, matching this patient's presentation.
(Choice D)
Bipolar I disorder
Bipolar I disorder requires at least one manic episode lasting at least 1 week (or requiring hospitalization) with symptoms like grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, and reckless behavior severe enough to cause marked functional impairment or psychotic features. This patient's elevated mood periods are milder and shorter, representing subthreshold symptoms that do not meet full manic criteria.
(Choice E)
Persistent depressive disorder
Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) involves chronic depressed mood for at least 2 years (1 year in children/adolescents) with additional depressive symptoms but without periods of normal mood lasting more than 2 months. This patient has alternating periods of elevated/hypomanic-like symptoms interspersed with her low periods, which are inconsistent with the unipolar nature of persistent depressive disorder.

pages.question: A 28-year-old woman who recently gave birth vaginally presents to the emergency department with excruciating pain in the anal region that started suddenly 24 hours ago. She reports difficulty sitting and walking due to the pain, and notes a tender lump near her anus. On physical examination, there is a 1.5 cm bluish-purple, tense bulge located externally below the dentate line, which is exquisitely tender to palpation. She denies fever, rectal bleeding, or changes in bowel habits. What is the most appropriate management for this patient's condition?

answers.text:
Observation with stool softeners and topical analgesics
(43.75%)

Rubber band ligation of the hemorrhoid
(14.06%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This postpartum patient has developed a thrombosed external hemorrhoid, presenting with severe pain and a bluish-purple bulge below the dentate line. The timing of presentation (within 24-48 hours of symptom onset) and severity of pain indicate the need for prompt surgical intervention with external hemorrhoidectomy under local anesthesia. Conservative management would be appropriate for mild cases or those presenting after 72 hours. Procedures like rubber band ligation and infrared photocoagulation are designed for internal hemorrhoids above the dentate line and are contraindicated for external hemorrhoids. Antibiotics are unnecessary as this is a thrombotic rather than infectious process.
(Choice A)
Infrared photocoagulation
Infrared photocoagulation is an office-based procedure used for grade I-II internal hemorrhoids to cause coagulation and sclerosis. It is not effective for thrombosed external hemorrhoids, which contain actual blood clots that require physical removal rather than coagulation therapy.
(Choice B)
Observation with stool softeners and topical analgesics
Conservative management with stool softeners and topical analgesics is appropriate for mild thrombosed external hemorrhoids or those presenting beyond 72 hours when the acute inflammatory phase has passed. However, this patient has severe, debilitating pain within 24 hours of onset, making surgical intervention the preferred approach for rapid pain relief.
(Choice C)
Hemorrhoidectomy under local anesthesia
For thrombosed external hemorrhoids causing severe pain, prompt excisional hemorrhoidectomy under local anesthesia provides rapid pain relief and is the recommended intervention.
(Choice D)
Oral antibiotics and sitz baths
Oral antibiotics are not indicated as thrombosed external hemorrhoids are not infectious processes but rather vascular thrombotic events. While warm sitz baths can provide symptomatic relief and are part of conservative management, they alone cannot resolve the underlying thrombosis causing severe pain in this acute presentation.
(Choice E)
Rubber band ligation of the hemorrhoid
Rubber band ligation is used for internal hemorrhoids above the dentate line and is contraindicated for external hemorrhoids due to the risk of severe pain and complications from somatic nerve involvement.

pages.question: A 62-year-old woman with a history of coronary artery disease and stable angina presents to the clinic for follow-up. She reports that her exertional chest pain has been well-controlled since starting isosorbide mononitrate therapy. The primary physiologic effect of this medication that alleviates her angina symptoms is:

answers.text:
Enhanced myocardial oxygen supply via angiogenesis
(4.84%)

Direct inhibition of smooth muscle contraction in coronary arteries
(30.65%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Nitrates act primarily as systemic vasodilators, lowering preload and left ventricular end-diastolic volume, which reduces myocardial oxygen demand and alleviates angina symptoms.
(Choice A)
Decreased left ventricular end-diastolic volume
This is correct. Nitrates primarily cause systemic venodilation, which reduces preload and left ventricular end-diastolic volume, thereby decreasing myocardial wall stress and oxygen demand.
(Choice B)
Enhanced myocardial oxygen supply via angiogenesis
This is incorrect. Nitrates do not promote arteriogenesis; their main effect is on preload reduction rather than enhancing oxygen supply through new vessel formation.
(Choice C)
Decreased heart rate
This is incorrect. Nitrates do not primarily affect heart rate; beta-blockers are more associated with heart rate reduction in angina management.
(Choice D)
Decreased systemic vascular resistance
This is incorrect. While nitrates do cause some arterial dilation at higher doses, leading to reduced afterload, their primary antianginal benefit comes from venodilation and preload reduction rather than arterial effects on systemic vascular resistance.
(Choice E)
Direct inhibition of smooth muscle contraction in coronary arteries
This is incorrect. While nitrates do relax coronary artery smooth muscle through their nitric oxide mechanism, the primary antianginal effect is achieved through systemic venodilation reducing preload, not through direct coronary artery effects.

pages.question: A 28-year-old primigravida at 32 weeks' gestation presents to her obstetrician with a 2-week history of gradually worsening low back pain. She works as a retail clerk and notes the pain is most severe at the end of her shifts after prolonged standing. The pain does not radiate and is relieved somewhat by lying down. She denies any urinary symptoms, vaginal bleeding, contractions, or weakness in her legs. On examination, she has mild tenderness over the lumbar paraspinal muscles, normal deep tendon reflexes, and negative straight-leg raise test. Fetal heart tones are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

answers.text:
Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Low back pain is common in the third trimester of pregnancy due to postural changes from uterine enlargement, weakened abdominal muscles, and joint/ligament laxity. In the absence of neurologic deficits or red flag symptoms, conservative management including reassurance, exercise, heating pads, and massage is recommended. Risk factors include occupations requiring prolonged standing.
(Choice A)
Strict bed rest for 2 weeks
Bed rest is contraindicated for mechanical low back pain as it leads to deconditioning, muscle weakening, and potentially worsens pain. Activity as tolerated with appropriate modifications is the recommended approach for pregnancy-related back pain.
(Choice B)
Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine
MRI is not indicated for mechanical low back pain without red flags (neurologic deficits, bowel/bladder dysfunction, fever, or progressive weakness). While MRI is safe in pregnancy after the first trimester, it would not change management for typical pregnancy-related back pain and is not cost-effective.
(Choice C)
Prescription of opioid analgesics
Opioids are not first-line treatment for pregnancy-related back pain. Acetaminophen is the preferred analgesic in pregnancy, and non-pharmacologic measures (physical therapy, prenatal massage, heat application) should be prioritized. Opioids carry risks of neonatal abstinence syndrome and respiratory depression.
(Choice D)
Reassurance and conservative management
This patient's symptoms are consistent with mechanical low back pain due to pregnancy-related changes, with no red flags. Conservative measures such as exercise, heat application, and posture education are appropriate.
(Choice E)
Referral to orthopedic surgery
Orthopedic referral is unnecessary for typical pregnancy-related mechanical back pain. Referral would be indicated only if red flags were present (neurologic deficits, suspected fracture, cauda equina syndrome) or if conservative management fails after an appropriate trial period.

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient's acute onset of severe back pain radiating to the groin, hemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia), pulsatile abdominal mass, and flank ecchymosis (Grey Turner's sign) are classic findings for ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). The retroperitoneal hemorrhage from AAA rupture causes the characteristic flank bruising and can lead to rapid hemodynamic compromise. The elevated lactate indicates tissue hypoperfusion consistent with hemorrhagic shock. Other diagnoses lack the combination of pulsatile mass and retroperitoneal bleeding signs.
(Choice A)
Acute severe pancreatitis
Acute pancreatitis typically presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back with nausea and vomiting. While severe hemorrhagic pancreatitis can cause hemodynamic instability, it would not produce a pulsatile abdominal mass or isolated flank ecchymosis. Expected laboratory findings would include elevated amylase and lipase levels.
(Choice B)
Type B aortic dissection
Aortic dissection typically presents with sudden, severe, tearing chest or back pain. While Type B dissection can cause back pain, it rarely presents with a pulsatile abdominal mass or flank ecchymosis. Patients often have hypertension rather than hypotension, and pulse deficits or neurologic symptoms may be present.
(Choice C)
Renal colic
Renal colic classically presents with sudden onset of severe unilateral flank pain radiating to the groin, often with hematuria and urinary urgency. However, it does not cause hemodynamic instability, pulsatile abdominal masses, or flank ecchymosis unless complicated by significant hemorrhage, which is extremely uncommon.
(Choice D)
Perforated peptic ulcer
Perforated peptic ulcer typically causes sudden, severe epigastric pain that may radiate to the back, with signs of peritonitis including abdominal rigidity and rebound tenderness. It does not produce a pulsatile abdominal mass, flank ecchymosis, or the specific pain radiation pattern described. Free air under the diaphragm would be visible on upright chest X-ray.
(Choice E)
Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm
This matches the presentation of acute severe pain, hemodynamic instability, pulsatile mass, and flank ecchymosis indicative of retroperitoneal hemorrhage from AAA rupture.

pages.question: A 28-year-old woman is admitted to the burn intensive care unit after sustaining extensive thermal burns from a gas explosion in her kitchen. She has second- and third-degree burns covering approximately 35% of her total body surface area, including her abdomen, back, and lower extremities. After securing her airway and initiating pain management, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation is started based on the Parkland formula. To ensure accurate monitoring of resuscitation efficacy, which of the following interventions should be performed as soon as possible?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Patients with major burns (>20% TBSA) require aggressive fluid resuscitation, and urethral catheterization is essential for precise measurement of urine output to guide therapy and prevent complications like acute kidney injury.
(Choice A)
Arterial blood gas analysis
Arterial blood gas analysis can assess acid-base status, oxygenation, and detect complications like carbon monoxide poisoning in burn patients, but it does not provide direct monitoring of fluid resuscitation adequacy, which is best assessed through urine output measurement.
(Choice B)
Urethral catheterization
Urethral catheterization allows for accurate hourly urine output measurement, which is critical to guide fluid resuscitation in patients with major burns to achieve a target of 0.5-1 mL/kg/hour and prevent under- or over-resuscitation.
(Choice C)
Echocardiography
Echocardiography can evaluate cardiac function and may be useful if cardiac complications are suspected, but it is not routinely indicated for initial burn resuscitation monitoring. Urine output provides a more practical and reliable endpoint for assessing adequate tissue perfusion.
(Choice D)
Immediate wound debridement
While wound debridement is important for preventing infection and will be performed within 24-48 hours, it is not the immediate priority after initial stabilization. The focus should first be on establishing accurate monitoring of fluid resuscitation to prevent complications.
(Choice E)
Central venous line placement
While central venous access may be needed for large-volume resuscitation and can provide central venous pressure monitoring, it is not the primary method for assessing fluid resuscitation adequacy in burn patients. Urine output remains the gold standard endpoint for guiding fluid therapy in burn resuscitation.

pages.question: A 16-year-old Asian male comes to the clinic with concerns about frequent breakouts on his face. He describes these as "small bumps" without significant redness. On physical examination, multiple open and closed comedones are noted. There is no significant inflammatory process observed. His medical history is unremarkable, and he doesn't have any significant lifestyle factors like smoking or alcohol consumption. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient's condition?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The initial management of acne depends on the predominant lesion type. Non-inflammatory comedonal acne results from abnormal follicular keratinization leading to microcomedo formation. Topical retinoids are first-line therapy because they normalize desquamation and prevent comedone formation by reducing follicular hyperkeratinization. Patients should be counseled about gradual improvement over 6-12 weeks and potential initial irritation that typically subsides with continued use.
(Choice A)
Benzoyl peroxide
Benzoyl peroxide is primarily effective for inflammatory acne due to its antimicrobial properties against P. acnes bacteria. While it has some comedolytic effects, topical retinoids are more effective for non-inflammatory comedonal acne as first-line therapy.
(Choice B)
Topical retinoids
Topical retinoids are the primary treatment for non-inflammatory acne with comedones. They help normalize the desquamation process to prevent clogged pores.
(Choice C)
Salicylic acid
Salicylic acid is a beta-hydroxy acid with mild comedolytic properties that can help with comedonal acne. However, topical retinoids are superior as first-line therapy for non-inflammatory acne due to their more potent effects on normalizing follicular keratinization.
(Choice D)
Antibiotic creams
Topical antibiotics (such as clindamycin or erythromycin) are effective for inflammatory acne due to their antimicrobial activity against P. acnes. They have minimal effect on comedone formation and are not indicated as monotherapy for non-inflammatory comedonal acne.
(Choice E)
Oral contraceptives
Oral contraceptives can help regulate hormonal acne in females but are not used in adolescent males and aren't the treatment of choice for comedones.

pages.question:
A 14-month-old uncircumcised boy is brought to the clinic with a 3-day history of high fever, irritability, and foul-smelling urine. His parents report decreased appetite and occasional vomiting. Vital signs include temperature of 102.4°F (39.1°C), heart rate 138 bpm, and blood pressure 90/55 mm Hg. Physical examination reveals mild suprapubic tenderness. Urinalysis is shown below. Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic therapy for this patient?



Urine pH	7.5
Leukocyte esterase	Positive
Nitrites	Positive
Urine white blood cells	80/HPF	(Normal: 0-2/HPF)
Urine microscopy	Gram-negative rods seen
Urine culture	Pending
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Urinary tract infections in young children, particularly uncircumcised boys, can present with fever, irritability, foul-smelling urine, and systemic symptoms. Positive nitrites and leukocyte esterase on urinalysis strongly suggest a UTI caused by gram-negative bacteria like Escherichia coli. Empiric treatment with a third-generation cephalosporin such as cefixime is recommended while awaiting culture results.
(Choice A)
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is an alternative for UTIs but has high rates of resistance among Escherichia coli strains in many regions, making it less ideal for empiric therapy without susceptibility data.
(Choice B)
Amoxicillin
Amoxicillin has poor coverage against gram-negative bacteria commonly causing UTIs, particularly E. coli, due to widespread beta-lactamase production. It would be ineffective against the gram-negative rods seen on microscopy and is not recommended for empiric UTI treatment in children.
(Choice C)
Ciprofloxacin
Ciprofloxacin is contraindicated in children under 18 years due to risk of cartilage damage and tendon rupture. Fluoroquinolones are reserved for complicated UTIs when other options have failed or based on culture sensitivities, not for empiric therapy in pediatric patients.
(Choice D)
Cefixime
Cefixime is a third-generation cephalosporin that provides excellent coverage against gram-negative bacteria, including Escherichia coli, the most common cause of pediatric UTIs. It is suitable for empiric oral therapy in stable outpatients.
(Choice E)
Nitrofurantoin
Nitrofurantoin is contraindicated in infants under 1 month and patients with suspected pyelonephritis. This patient's fever, systemic symptoms, and suprapubic tenderness suggest upper tract involvement where nitrofurantoin achieves inadequate tissue concentrations and would be ineffective.

pages.question: A 72-year-old man with a history of diabetes and hyperlipidemia is brought to the emergency department after collapsing at home. He reports acute onset of substernal chest pain, shortness of breath, and dizziness prior to the event. On examination, his blood pressure is 82/48 mmHg, heart rate is 105 bpm, and respiratory rate is 22 breaths/min. He has prominent jugular venous distension, clear lung fields, and cool extremities. An electrocardiogram is shown. Echocardiography shows akinesis of the inferior left ventricular wall and dilation of the right ventricle with reduced systolic function. Intravenous fluids are administered, resulting in partial improvement of his blood pressure. What is the primary mechanism responsible for this patient's hypotension?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient has an inferior wall ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (MI) with right ventricular involvement (RVMI), leading to decreased right ventricular contractility. This impairs right ventricular output, reducing left ventricular preload and causing hypotension, which is preload-dependent and often responsive to volume expansion. Jugular venous distension reflects elevated right-sided filling pressures, while clear lungs indicate preserved left ventricular function. ECG shows ST segment elevation in the inferior leads with Q waves in leads III and aVF, consistent with acute inferior wall myocardial infarction.
(Choice A)
Decreased right ventricular contractility
This is correct. In right ventricular myocardial infarction (RVMI), often complicating inferior wall MI, reduced RV contractility leads to decreased RV output, impairing LV preload and causing hypotension. The condition is preload-dependent, explaining the response to fluids and signs like jugular venous distension.
(Choice B)
Vasodilatory shock from sepsis
This is incorrect. The clinical presentation (acute chest pain, ECG changes consistent with MI, echocardiographic findings of wall motion abnormalities) clearly indicates a cardiogenic cause rather than septic shock. Additionally, vasodilatory shock would typically present with warm extremities and low systemic vascular resistance, not the cool extremities seen here.
(Choice C)
Elevated pulmonary vascular resistance
This is incorrect. In acute right ventricular myocardial infarction, the primary problem is not elevated pulmonary vascular resistance but rather intrinsic RV pump failure. The RV cannot effectively pump blood forward, leading to reduced cardiac output and systemic hypotension, without significant changes in pulmonary vascular resistance.
(Choice D)
Decreased left ventricular contractility
This is incorrect. While the inferior wall MI does cause some left ventricular dysfunction, the primary mechanism of hypotension in this scenario is right ventricular failure. The key clinical clues are jugular venous distension with clear lung fields and fluid responsiveness - findings characteristic of isolated RV dysfunction rather than primary LV failure.
(Choice E)
Hypovolemia from dehydration
This is incorrect. Although hypotension improves with fluids, the underlying cause is not absolute hypovolemia but rather preload dependence due to RV dysfunction in RVMI, with elevated right-sided pressures indicated by jugular distension.

pages.question:
A 45-year-old engineer visits the outpatient clinic complaining of persistent weakness, mild abdominal discomfort, and unexplained weight loss. He has a history of alcohol use disorder and hepatitis B. His lifestyle includes regular consumption of tobacco and recreational drugs. On examination, mild jaundice and abdominal tenderness are noted. Laboratory results include:

Liver studies:
- Albumin: 3.2 g/dL
- Total bilirubin: 2.1 mg/dL
- Direct bilirubin: 0.9 mg/dL
- Alkaline phosphatase: 110 IU/L
- Aspartate aminotransferase (AST): 255 IU/L
- Alanine aminotransferase (ALT): 205 IU/L

Coagulation profile:
- Prothrombin time (PT): 14 sec
- Partial thromboplastin time (PTT): 30 sec

Tests show positive Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg). A few days into supportive therapy, tests reveal an increase in PT and a notable decrease in AST and ALT levels. What underlying condition do these changes suggest?

answers.text:
Resolution stage of hepatitis B infection
(47.52%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The paradoxical combination of decreasing transaminase levels with increasing PT is a classic sign of acute liver failure. While falling AST/ALT might seem reassuring, it actually indicates massive hepatocyte death - fewer viable cells remain to release enzymes. The rising PT reflects impaired hepatic synthetic function, confirming severe liver dysfunction despite the 'improving' transaminases.
(Choice A)
Benign liver cysts
Such cysts rarely affect liver function tests unless compressing major ducts.
(Choice B)
Hepatitis D co-infection
Hepatitis D co-infection would typically cause persistently elevated or rising transaminase levels due to ongoing hepatocellular damage. The pattern of falling AST/ALT with rising PT is not consistent with active viral co-infection.
(Choice C)
Hepatitis C contagion
Hepatitis C co-infection would cause elevated transaminase levels due to ongoing viral hepatitis. The decreasing AST/ALT pattern seen here is inconsistent with active viral hepatitis from any cause.
(Choice D)
Resolution stage of hepatitis B infection
In true recovery from hepatitis B, transaminase levels decrease while PT remains stable or improves. The combination of falling transaminases with a worsening PT indicates liver failure, not recovery.
(Choice E)
Acute liver failure
A prolonged PT with paradoxically decreasing AST and ALT levels indicates acute liver failure. While falling transaminases might suggest improvement, they actually reflect massive hepatocyte necrosis - fewer viable cells remain to release enzymes. The rising PT indicates impaired synthetic function, a hallmark of acute liver failure.

pages.question: A 65-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of progressive fatigue, unintentional weight loss, and early satiety. Over the past week, he has developed severe pain and swelling in his left ankle, making it difficult to bear weight. Physical examination reveals pallor, massive splenomegaly, and a warm, erythematous, and tender left ankle joint. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, platelet count 120,000/μL, white blood cell count 18,000/μL with a left shift, and serum uric acid 12.5 mg/dL. A peripheral blood smear demonstrates teardrop-shaped red blood cells and immature myeloid precursors. Synovial fluid aspiration from the ankle reveals numerous negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals under polarized light microscopy. This patient's acute arthritis is most likely a complication of which of the following conditions?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient presents with classic findings of primary myelofibrosis (massive splenomegaly, cytopenias, leukoerythroblastic blood smear with teardrop cells) complicated by acute gouty arthritis. The myeloproliferative disorder causes hyperuricemia through increased purine turnover from excessive myeloid cell proliferation and breakdown, leading to urate crystal deposition in the joint.
(Choice A)
Hemolytic anemia
While hemolytic anemia can lead to hyperuricemia from increased cell turnover and nucleotide breakdown, the clinical presentation here is inconsistent with isolated hemolytic anemia. The massive splenomegaly, teardrop cells, and leukoerythroblastic blood smear with immature myeloid precursors indicate bone marrow pathology with extramedullary hematopoiesis rather than simple red cell destruction.
(Choice B)
Psoriasis
Psoriasis can be associated with hyperuricemia due to increased skin cell turnover, but it does not cause the hematologic abnormalities, splenomegaly, or bone marrow findings observed in this case.
(Choice C)
Myeloproliferative disorder
Myeloproliferative disorders, particularly primary myelofibrosis, cause hyperuricemia through multiple mechanisms: excessive proliferation and turnover of myeloid cells leads to increased purine breakdown and uric acid production. The clinical presentation is classic for myelofibrosis: massive splenomegaly due to extramedullary hematopoiesis, cytopenias from bone marrow fibrosis, and a leukoerythroblastic blood smear with teardrop cells and immature myeloid precursors. The resulting hyperuricemia predisposes to acute gouty arthritis.
(Choice D)
Lymphoproliferative disorder
While lymphoproliferative disorders can cause hyperuricemia due to increased cell turnover and tumor lysis, the clinical picture is more consistent with a myeloid rather than lymphoid process. The presence of immature myeloid precursors in the peripheral blood, teardrop cells, and massive splenomegaly suggest myelofibrosis with extramedullary hematopoiesis. Lymphomas typically present with lymphadenopathy and would not produce this specific leukoerythroblastic blood picture.
(Choice E)
Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism is associated with hyperuricemia in some cases due to decreased renal clearance, but it does not explain the splenomegaly, anemia, or abnormal blood smear findings seen in this patient.

pages.question: During a 12-year-old boy's annual well-child visit, his pediatrician calculates his BMI at 27.5 kg/m², which plots at the 91st percentile for his age and sex. His mother asks what this means and what changes they should make at home. She reports he typically drinks two 20-oz sports drinks and one juice box daily, eats fast food three times per week, and watches television or plays video games for approximately 4–5 hours per day after school. He has no symptoms and his physical exam is unremarkable. Fasting labs drawn at a prior visit show a mildly elevated ALT of 38 U/L (normal <35 U/L) and normal fasting glucose. Which of the following counseling statements is most appropriate for this family?

answers.text:
He should eliminate sugar-sweetened and high-calorie beverages, limit recreational screen time to 2 hours per day, and increase physical activity, with the whole family making these changes together
(0%)

Recommend that he exercise for at least 2 hours per day and restrict all carbohydrate intake
(0%)

Refer him immediately to a pediatric bariatric surgeon for weight loss surgery evaluation
(0%)

His BMI is within the normal range for his age, so no dietary changes are necessary at this time
(0%)

Begin a strict low-calorie diet of fewer than 1,200 kcal/day to promote rapid weight loss
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
A BMI between the 85th and 94th percentile defines overweight in children, which warrants proactive counseling before obesity develops. Key modifiable targets include elimination of sugar-sweetened and high-calorie beverages (sports drinks, juice), limiting recreational screen time to 2 hours per day, increasing physical activity, and emphasizing whole foods. Family-centered counseling is more effective than child-directed advice alone, as parents control the home food and activity environment.
(Choice A)
He should eliminate sugar-sweetened and high-calorie beverages, limit recreational screen time to 2 hours per day, and increase physical activity, with the whole family making these changes together
This boy's BMI at the 91st percentile classifies him as overweight (85th–94th percentile), which warrants proactive, family-centered lifestyle counseling to prevent progression to obesity. Sports drinks and fruit juices are high in sugar and calories and provide no nutritional advantage over water; elimination of these beverages is one of the most impactful dietary changes a family can make. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends limiting recreational screen time to no more than 2 hours per day for school-aged children, as excessive screen time is associated with sedentary behavior, disrupted sleep, and increased exposure to food advertising. Physical activity of at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity per day is recommended for children. Family-centered counseling is essential because children's dietary and activity behaviors are largely determined by the home environment, and interventions that engage parents as active participants yield significantly better outcomes than child-directed advice alone. The mildly elevated ALT may reflect early hepatic steatosis and reinforces the importance of lifestyle modification. Goals should be realistic and incremental — focusing on behavior change rather than weight loss targets in growing children.
(Choice B)
Recommend that he exercise for at least 2 hours per day and restrict all carbohydrate intake
While increasing physical activity is appropriate, recommending 2 hours of daily exercise is excessive and not aligned with evidence-based pediatric guidelines, which recommend 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily. Such unrealistic expectations may discourage participation and lead to burnout. Complete carbohydrate restriction is not evidence-based in pediatric populations and may compromise energy availability needed for growth, brain development, and physical activity. Additionally, restrictive diets can lead to disordered eating patterns in children. Dietary counseling should emphasize eliminating nutrient-poor, high-calorie foods while maintaining balanced macronutrient intake.
(Choice C)
Refer him immediately to a pediatric bariatric surgeon for weight loss surgery evaluation
Bariatric surgery is not appropriate for a 12-year-old who is classified as overweight (not obese) and has no severe comorbidities. Surgical evaluation in pediatric patients is generally reserved for adolescents with severe obesity (BMI ≥35 or ≥120% of the 95th percentile) and significant obesity-related comorbidities after failure of sustained lifestyle intervention. Referral at this stage would be premature and inconsistent with evidence-based pediatric obesity guidelines.
(Choice D)
His BMI is within the normal range for his age, so no dietary changes are necessary at this time
A BMI at the 91st percentile for age and sex falls in the overweight category (85th–94th percentile), not the normal range (5th–84th percentile). This distinction is clinically important because children who are overweight have a significantly increased risk of progressing to obesity and developing associated comorbidities such as type 2 diabetes, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, and cardiovascular risk factors. The mildly elevated ALT in this case may already indicate early hepatic steatosis. Reassurance without intervention at this stage represents a missed opportunity for prevention through family-centered lifestyle counseling.
(Choice E)
Begin a strict low-calorie diet of fewer than 1,200 kcal/day to promote rapid weight loss
Severe caloric restriction in a growing child can impair normal growth, pubertal development, and nutrient adequacy. For overweight children, the goal is typically weight maintenance or slowing the rate of weight gain as the child grows taller, rather than active weight loss. Dietary counseling should focus on improving food quality — eliminating caloric beverages, reducing fast food, and increasing fruits, vegetables, and whole grains — rather than imposing strict caloric limits that are difficult to sustain and potentially harmful in pediatric patients.

pages.question: An 8-year-old Hispanic girl is rushed to the children's hospital following a sudden Oset of excruciating headache followed by episodes of vomiting and confusion. Her body temperature is 37 C (98.6 F), blood pressure measures 128/75 mm Hg, heart rate is 62/min, and her respiratory rate is 20/min. On examination, she displays neck stiffness, but no other neurological deficits. A CT scan of the brain reveals evidence of bleeding in the subarachnoid space. Which of the following is the most likely additional clinical finding in this patient?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The sudden onset of severe headache, vomiting, altered mental states, and a CT-confirmed subarachnoid hemorrhage in this young girl suggest an AVM rupture. Such malformations can elicit seizure episodes, providing a diagnostic clue to their presence before a rupture occurs. These cases often lack the focal neurological deficits observed in other hemorrhagic or traumatic brain injuries.
(Choice A)
History of head trauma
Recent head trauma typically causes epidural or subdural hemorrhages rather than subarachnoid hemorrhage. Traumatic SAH usually occurs in the setting of severe head injury with other signs of trauma. The acute onset of severe headache without focal deficits in this case is more consistent with spontaneous SAH from vascular malformation rather than trauma.
(Choice B)
Developmental delay
Developmental delay is not a typical preceding feature of arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) that cause subarachnoid hemorrhage. While some complex vascular malformations can be associated with developmental issues, isolated AVMs causing SAH typically do not present with developmental delay as a warning sign.
(Choice C)
Coagulopathy or bleeding disorder
Coagulopathies typically cause diffuse bleeding or bleeding into multiple sites rather than the focal subarachnoid hemorrhage seen here. Additionally, bleeding disorders usually present with other bleeding manifestations (bruising, petechiae, or mucosal bleeding) and would not typically cause the sudden, isolated subarachnoid hemorrhage pattern characteristic of AVM rupture.
(Choice D)
Previous episodes of seizures
The girl's presentation is consistent with subarachnoid hemorrhage, characterized by sudden headache, vomiting, and altered consciousness. A common cause in children is arteriovenous malformation (AVM) rupture. AVMs can cause seizures, recurring headaches, or migraines prior to rupture. Thus, a history of seizures would fit the clinical picture and assist in the diagnosis.
(Choice E)
Cardiac anomalies
While certain cardiac anomalies can be associated with vascular malformations in rare syndromic conditions, isolated arteriovenous malformations causing subarachnoid hemorrhage are not typically preceded by cardiac anomalies. Cardiac defects are more relevant to embolic strokes than spontaneous hemorrhagic events from AVMs.

pages.question: A 13-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her parents due to concerns about delayed menstruation. The parents note that the girl's breasts started developing approximately 20 months ago, and she has developed some axillary and pubic hair over the past year. She has experienced a recent growth spurt, gaining 4 inches in height over the last 8 months. The girl is active in sports, maintains a healthy diet, and has no chronic medical conditions or medication use. Physical examination shows Tanner stage 3 breast development, Tanner stage 3 pubic hair, and normal vital signs. The parents are worried because a cousin had early puberty issues. Which of the following is the most appropriate management at this time?

answers.text:
Reassurance and reevaluation if menarche does not occur by age 15
(96.05%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This 13-year-old girl demonstrates normal pubertal progression with breast development starting about 20 months ago, followed by pubic hair and a growth spurt. Menarche typically follows thelarche by 2-2.5 years and occurs around Tanner stage 4 breast development. As she is under 15 years old with normal breast and pubic hair development, no further evaluation is needed at this time. Reassurance and reevaluation if menarche does not occur by age 15 is appropriate. Diagnostic tests such as brain MRI, karyotype, pelvic ultrasound, serum estradiol, or thyroid studies are not indicated without signs of abnormal puberty or primary amenorrhea.
(Choice A)
Serum estradiol measurement
Serum estradiol measurement is not needed as clinical examination already demonstrates adequate estrogenization (breast development, growth spurt). Hormone levels would be considered if there were signs of delayed puberty or if menarche has not occurred by age 15.
(Choice B)
Brain MRI
Brain MRI is not indicated as this patient shows normal pubertal progression. Brain MRI would be considered for precocious puberty (onset before age 8 in girls) or delayed puberty (no breast development by age 13 or no menarche by age 15), neither of which applies to this case.
(Choice C)
Karyotype analysis
Karyotype analysis is not indicated as this patient demonstrates normal pubertal development. Karyotyping would be considered for primary amenorrhea after age 15 with absent secondary sexual characteristics or signs suggestive of Turner syndrome (short stature, webbed neck, widely spaced nipples).
(Choice D)
Reassurance and reevaluation if menarche does not occur by age 15
This is the correct approach as the patient's pubertal development is normal, and menarche is expected within the typical timeframe without need for intervention before age 15.
(Choice E)
Thyroid function tests
Thyroid function tests are not warranted without clinical evidence of thyroid dysfunction or delayed puberty beyond expected norms.

pages.question: A 28-year-old woman at 32 weeks gestation presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of fever to 38.9°C, myalgias, headache, and mild neck stiffness. She denies nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Her husband reports that she has been eating soft cheeses and deli meats purchased from a local farmers market over the past week. Vital signs: temperature 38.9°C, heart rate 102 bpm, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min. Lumbar puncture reveals: WBC 210 cells/µL (80% monocytes), protein 68 mg/dL, glucose 44 mg/dL (serum glucose 92 mg/dL). Blood cultures are pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen for this patient?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Listeria monocytogenes should be suspected in pregnant women who develop febrile illness or meningitis after consuming unpasteurized dairy products or deli meats. CSF classically shows a monocytic pleocytosis. Ampicillin is the drug of choice because Listeria is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins, which are commonly used for community-acquired meningitis in immunocompetent adults.
(Choice A)
Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone
Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone is the standard empiric regimen for community-acquired bacterial meningitis targeting S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis. However, neither agent covers Listeria monocytogenes, which is intrinsically cephalosporin-resistant and not reliably covered by vancomycin. This regimen would be inadequate for a pregnant patient with suspected Listeria infection.
(Choice B)
Ceftriaxone alone
Ceftriaxone is the backbone of empiric bacterial meningitis therapy for most pathogens but has no activity against Listeria monocytogenes due to intrinsic resistance mediated by low-affinity penicillin-binding proteins. Using ceftriaxone alone in a pregnant patient with suspected Listeria meningitis would result in treatment failure and potential fetal loss.
(Choice C)
Ampicillin plus gentamicin
Listeria monocytogenes is the most likely pathogen given the clinical context of a pregnant woman who consumed unpasteurized dairy and deli meats, presenting with febrile meningitis and a monocyte-predominant CSF pleocytosis. Listeria is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins due to its low-affinity penicillin-binding proteins, making ampicillin the cornerstone of therapy. Gentamicin is added for synergistic bactericidal activity, particularly important in immunocompromised hosts such as pregnant women, neonates, and the elderly. Pregnancy itself represents a state of relative T-cell immunosuppression that markedly increases susceptibility to intracellular pathogens like Listeria, which can cross the placental barrier and cause fetal infection, stillbirth, or neonatal sepsis. This combination is the standard of care per IDSA guidelines for Listeria meningitis. Dexamethasone, if given, should be discontinued if Listeria is confirmed, as it is not beneficial for this pathogen.
(Choice D)
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole alone
TMP-SMX is an alternative agent for Listeria in penicillin-allergic patients and has good CNS penetration. However, it is not recommended as first-line monotherapy in a critically ill pregnant patient with active meningitis where synergistic bactericidal activity is needed. Additionally, TMP-SMX is generally avoided in late pregnancy (particularly near term) due to theoretical concerns about folate antagonism affecting fetal development, though this is less concerning at 32 weeks than the inadequate monotherapy for severe CNS infection.
(Choice E)
Acyclovir plus ceftriaxone
Acyclovir plus ceftriaxone would be appropriate empiric therapy if herpes simplex encephalitis were high on the differential, typically presenting with temporal lobe involvement, behavioral changes, and focal neurologic deficits. While HSV can affect pregnant women, the dietary exposure history, monocytic CSF pleocytosis, and systemic myalgias are much more consistent with Listeria monocytogenes. Acyclovir alone does not cover bacterial causes of meningitis.

pages.question: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic by his parents due to concerns about his social interactions and behaviors. The parents note that he has an intense fascination with trains, spending hours watching videos of them and memorizing schedules, but he refuses to play with toy trains in any imaginative way with peers. He does not initiate conversations with other children at daycare and often ignores them when they approach him. He insists on following the same path to school every day and becomes inconsolable if there is any deviation. Additionally, he frequently flaps his hands when excited and has delayed expressive language skills, using short phrases rather than full sentences. His hearing and vision screenings are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This child's intense fixation on trains, lack of social initiation, rigid adherence to routines, hand flapping, and language delay are characteristic of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). ASD typically presents in early childhood with deficits in social communication, repetitive behaviors, and restricted interests, and is more prevalent in males.
(Choice A)
Autism spectrum disorder
The patient's symptoms, including impaired social interactions, restricted interests in trains, repetitive hand flapping, rigid routines, and language delay, align with the diagnostic criteria for autism spectrum disorder, which manifests in early childhood.
(Choice B)
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
ADHD typically involves inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity as core symptoms. While children with ADHD may have social difficulties, these are secondary to the primary symptoms and do not include the characteristic repetitive behaviors, restricted interests, or the degree of social communication deficits seen in this case.
(Choice C)
Intellectual disability
Intellectual disability presents with global delays in cognitive and adaptive functioning, but does not specifically include the social deficits, repetitive behaviors, and restricted interests observed in this case.
(Choice D)
Social communication disorder
Social (pragmatic) communication disorder involves persistent difficulties with social use of verbal and nonverbal communication. However, by definition, it excludes cases where repetitive behaviors and restricted interests are present, which would instead point toward autism spectrum disorder.
(Choice E)
Early-onset schizophrenia
Childhood-onset schizophrenia is rare and features hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking, which are not described in this patient's presentation of social and behavioral symptoms.

pages.question:
A 52-year-old male professor presents to the clinic with a 10-day history of low-grade fever, fatigue, palpitations, and sharp pain in the anterior neck radiating to the jaw, which worsens when he turns his head or swallows. He denies any recent trauma but recalls having a mild flu-like illness with cough and runny nose about three weeks ago during a university outbreak. On physical examination, his temperature is 37.8°C, heart rate is 105 bpm, and there is mild tremor in his outstretched hands. The thyroid gland is diffusely enlarged, firm, and exquisitely tender to palpation without any nodules or bruits. Laboratory evaluation is shown below. A thyroid ultrasound shows heterogeneous echotexture without abscess or nodules, and radioactive iodine uptake is markedly decreased at 2% (normal: 8-30%). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?



WBC Count	7200 /µL
Neutrophils	60 %
Lymphocytes	30 %
Monocytes	6 %
Eosinophils	3 %
Basophils	1 %
Hemoglobin	13.5 g/dL
Hematocrit	40 %
RBC Count	4.6 million/µL
Platelet Count	250000 /µL
TSH	0.02 mU/L
Free T4	2.8 ng/dL
Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)	95 mm/h
C-Reactive Protein (CRP)	45 mg/L
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient presents with painful thyrotoxicosis, fever, thyroid tenderness, elevated free T4 with suppressed TSH, elevated inflammatory markers, and low radioiodine uptake following a recent viral illness, consistent with subacute thyroiditis.
(Choice A)
Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis
Type 2 amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis is a destructive thyroiditis but requires a history of amiodarone use, which is absent here; it also typically lacks the prominent pain and post-viral association seen in subacute thyroiditis.
(Choice B)
Toxic multinodular goiter
Toxic multinodular goiter presents with painless hyperthyroidism from autonomous nodules, with normal or increased radioiodine uptake and often palpable nodules, not diffuse tenderness or elevated inflammatory markers.
(Choice C)
Hashimoto's thyroiditis
Hashimoto's thyroiditis typically presents as painless chronic thyroiditis leading to hypothyroidism over months to years, with positive antithyroid antibodies (anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin). It does not cause acute onset of pain, fever, or the initial hyperthyroid phase with low uptake seen here.
(Choice D)
Graves disease
Graves disease typically presents with painless hyperthyroidism, often with ophthalmopathy or pretibial myxedema, and shows increased radioiodine uptake (>30%) due to TSH receptor stimulation, not the decreased uptake (2%) seen in this case.
(Choice E)
Subacute thyroiditis
Subacute thyroiditis is characterized by painful thyroid inflammation following a viral infection, with initial hyperthyroidism due to follicular destruction, suppressed TSH, elevated free T4, high ESR/CRP, and low radioiodine uptake.

pages.question:
A 22-year-old college student presents with increasing fatigue, yellowing of the eyes, and occasional dark urine over the past 6 months. She reports that her symptoms worsen after viral illnesses. Her mother and maternal aunt both underwent splenectomy in their 30s for unspecified blood disorders. Physical examination reveals mild icterus and splenomegaly. Laboratory studies are shown below. A peripheral blood smear is obtained. Which of the following laboratory findings is most characteristic of this patient's underlying condition?



Hemoglobin	19 g/dL
RBC	6.2 ×10^12/L
Hematocrit	57 %
MCV	92 fL
MCH	31 pg
MCHC	33 g/dL
Platelets	500,000 /µL
WBC	7.8 ×10^9/L
Neutrophils	62 %
Lymphocytes	28 %
Monocytes	6 %
Eosinophils	3 %
Basophils	1 %
ALT	32 U/L
AST	30 U/L
Alkaline Phosphatase	160 U/L
Bilirubin Total	12 µmol/L
Bilirubin Direct	3 µmol/L
Albumin	44 g/L
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient has hereditary spherocytosis, an inherited membrane disorder characterized by hemolytic anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly, positive family history, and spherocytes on peripheral smear. The elevated mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (>37 g/dL) results from red blood cell membrane loss and dehydration, making it the most characteristic laboratory finding.
(Choice A)
Absent haptoglobin
This is incorrect. While low haptoglobin can occur in extravascular hemolysis like HS, it is not the most characteristic finding; elevated MCHC is more specific for HS among hemolytic anemias.
(Choice B)
Positive direct antiglobulin test
This is incorrect. A positive direct antiglobulin test (Coombs test) indicates autoimmune hemolytic anemia where antibodies coat red blood cells. Hereditary spherocytosis is a membrane disorder and is typically Coombs-negative.
(Choice C)
Decreased osmotic fragility
This is incorrect. Hereditary spherocytosis is associated with increased osmotic fragility due to membrane defects that make red cells more susceptible to hemolysis in hypotonic solutions.
(Choice D)
Low mean corpuscular volume
This is incorrect. In hereditary spherocytosis, MCV is typically normal to slightly decreased. The key finding is an elevated MCHC due to membrane loss and cellular dehydration, not a low MCV.
(Choice E)
Elevated mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration
This is correct. In hereditary spherocytosis, loss of red blood cell membrane leads to dehydration and an elevated MCHC, typically >37 g/dL (normal range 32-36 g/dL).

pages.question:
A 52-year-old woman with a history of calcium oxalate kidney stones presents to the emergency department with severe, intermittent right flank pain radiating to the groin that began 4 hours ago. She reports nausea but no vomiting, fever, or dysuria. Vital signs are normal. A non-contrast CT scan reveals a 7 mm stone in the distal right ureter with mild hydronephrosis. The patient is hemodynamically stable and has no evidence of renal dysfunction or infection. In addition to hydration and pain control, which of the following medications is most appropriate to facilitate passage of this stone?



White blood cell count	7600/mm3
Neutrophils	60%
Lymphocytes	30%
Monocytes	7%
Eosinophils	2%
Basophils	1%
Red blood cell count	4.6x10^6/µL
Hemoglobin	14.1 g/dL
Hematocrit	42%
Platelet count	248000/µL
Mean platelet volume	9.5 fL
Urine Color	Yellow	(range: Clear to yellow)
Urine Appearance	Clear	(normal: Clear)
Urine Specific Gravity	1.020	(range: 1.005–1.030)
Urine pH	6.0	(range: 4.5–8.0)
Urine Protein	Negative	(normal: Negative to trace)
Urine Blood	Positive	(normal: Negative)
Urine Red Blood Cells	5-10/HPF	(range: 0–2/HPF)
Urine White Blood Cells	0-2/HPF	(range: 0–5/HPF)
Leukocyte Esterase	Negative	(normal: Negative)
Nitrites	Negative	(normal: Negative)
Urine casts	None seen
Urine bacteria	None seen
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has acute ureteral colic due to a distal ureteral stone. For uncomplicated distal ureteral stones less than 10 mm, medical expulsive therapy with alpha-1 antagonists like tamsulosin is recommended to relax ureteral smooth muscle, decrease intraureteral pressure, and promote stone passage. This approach reduces the need for interventions and analgesics while maintaining conservative management.
(Choice A)
Oxybutynin
Oxybutynin is an anticholinergic used for bladder spasms but has no role in relaxing ureteral smooth muscle for stone expulsion.
(Choice B)
Allopurinol
Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor used for long-term prevention of uric acid stone recurrence by reducing uric acid production. It has no acute effect on ureteral smooth muscle tone and does not facilitate passage of existing stones.
(Choice C)
Ibuprofen
While ibuprofen is an important component of pain management in renal colic due to its analgesic and anti-inflammatory properties, it does not have the alpha-1 blocking properties needed to relax ureteral smooth muscle and facilitate stone passage.
(Choice D)
Tamsulosin
Tamsulosin is an alpha-1 antagonist that relaxes ureteral smooth muscle, decreases intraureteral pressure, and facilitates stone passage in distal ureteral calculi.
(Choice E)
Morphine
Morphine provides pain relief but does not affect ureteral tone or promote stone expulsion.

pages.question: A 52-year-old man presents with a 5-week history of right knee pain that began after he twisted his knee while stepping off a curb awkwardly during a walk. He reports intermittent sharp pain, especially when squatting or climbing stairs, along with a sensation of the knee 'catching' and occasional limitation in fully extending the joint. There is no significant swelling at present, and he has tried rest and over-the-counter analgesics with minimal relief. Physical examination reveals tenderness along the medial joint line and pain on hyperflexion, but no ligamentous instability. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient presents with classic signs of meniscal tear: knee pain with mechanical symptoms (catching, limited extension) following a twisting injury. The combination of medial joint line tenderness, pain on hyperflexion, and persistent symptoms beyond 3-4 weeks warrants MRI evaluation. MRI is the gold standard for diagnosing meniscal tears and guides treatment decisions between conservative management and surgical intervention. Plain radiographs evaluate bony pathology but miss soft tissue injuries. Arthrocentesis is reserved for suspected effusion or infection. Corticosteroid injection treats inflammatory conditions, not structural mechanical problems. Bone scan detects occult fractures or malignancy but provides no meniscal detail.
(Choice A)
Intra-articular corticosteroid injection
Intra-articular corticosteroid injections are appropriate for inflammatory conditions like osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis. However, this patient's acute mechanical symptoms (catching, limited extension) following trauma suggest a structural problem like meniscal tear that would not respond to anti-inflammatory treatment.
(Choice B)
Radionuclide bone scan
Bone scans are used to detect occult fractures, malignancy, or osteomyelitis, but they do not provide detailed information on soft tissue structures like the meniscus.
(Choice C)
Plain radiograph of the knee
Plain radiographs are useful for evaluating bony abnormalities, fractures, or osteoarthritis but are not sensitive for soft tissue injuries like meniscal tears. While X-rays might be considered as initial imaging, the clinical presentation strongly suggests meniscal pathology requiring soft tissue evaluation.
(Choice D)
MRI of the knee
MRI is the imaging modality of choice for evaluating suspected meniscal tears, especially with persistent symptoms and mechanical findings like catching or limited range of motion.
(Choice E)
Arthrocentesis of the knee joint
Arthrocentesis is indicated when there is joint effusion, suspected septic arthritis, or crystal arthropathy. This patient has no current swelling or signs of inflammation, and his symptoms (catching, mechanical locking) suggest structural mechanical pathology rather than inflammatory or infectious causes.

pages.question: A 78-year-old woman is brought to her primary care physician by her daughter, who is concerned that her mother has become progressively weaker over the past year. The patient reports eating less meat and dairy products due to dental problems and a reduced appetite. She lives alone and prepares simple meals. On examination, her BMI is 20.1 kg/m², grip strength is markedly reduced bilaterally, and she has difficulty rising from a chair without using her arms. Gait speed is 0.7 m/s. Laboratory studies show albumin 3.2 g/dL, prealbumin 14 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.5 mg/dL (low, consistent with reduced muscle mass). Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention to address the primary nutritional etiology of her functional decline?

answers.text:
Increase dietary protein intake to at least 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day and initiate resistance exercise
(75%)

Prescribe high-dose vitamin D supplementation only
(0%)

Initiate oral iron supplementation and obtain complete blood count
(25%)

Refer for total parenteral nutrition given her low prealbumin
(0%)

Start a high-calorie, high-fat oral nutritional supplement to increase BMI
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Sarcopenia in older adults results from inadequate protein intake combined with physical inactivity, leading to progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength, and function. Older adults require 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day of protein (higher than the 0.8 g/kg/day RDA for younger adults) due to anabolic resistance. Resistance exercise combined with adequate protein intake, particularly leucine-rich sources, is the most effective evidence-based intervention to prevent or reverse sarcopenia.
(Choice A)
Increase dietary protein intake to at least 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day and initiate resistance exercise
This patient's presentation is classic for sarcopenia: low BMI, reduced grip strength, difficulty rising from a chair, and slow gait speed (below the 0.8 m/s threshold), occurring in the context of severely reduced protein intake due to dental issues and anorexia. Sarcopenia is defined by loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength, and physical performance, and its primary nutritional driver in older adults is inadequate protein consumption. The general adult RDA of 0.8 g/kg/day is insufficient for older adults, who require 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day or more to maintain muscle protein synthesis, which is already blunted by anabolic resistance associated with aging. Protein supplementation — particularly with leucine-rich sources such as whey — stimulates muscle protein synthesis more effectively than other amino acid profiles. Resistance exercise is a critical adjunct because it restores anabolic signaling pathways (mTOR activation) in muscle, which further amplifies the effect of protein intake. Combined nutritional and exercise interventions have been shown in randomized trials to improve grip strength, gait speed, and functional independence in sarcopenic older adults. Addressing dental barriers to eating protein-rich foods (e.g., referral to dentistry, soft protein-rich foods) is also an important practical step in this patient.
(Choice B)
Prescribe high-dose vitamin D supplementation only
While vitamin D deficiency is common in older adults and can contribute to muscle weakness and falls, vitamin D supplementation alone does not address the primary driver of this patient's sarcopenia - inadequate protein intake combined with physical inactivity. Vitamin D should be assessed and repleted if deficient, but protein optimization and resistance exercise are the cornerstone interventions for sarcopenia management.
(Choice C)
Initiate oral iron supplementation and obtain complete blood count
While protein-energy malnutrition can cause low albumin, there is no evidence of iron deficiency anemia in this case (no hemoglobin or hematocrit values provided, and low creatinine suggests reduced muscle mass rather than anemia). Iron supplementation would not address the primary problem of sarcopenia from inadequate protein intake. The patient's functional decline is due to muscle wasting, not iron deficiency.
(Choice D)
Refer for total parenteral nutrition given her low prealbumin
Parenteral nutrition is reserved for patients with non-functional gastrointestinal tracts or severe malabsorption who cannot meet nutritional needs enterally. This patient is able to eat orally, and her nutritional deficits are due to inadequate intake and food access issues rather than malabsorption or gut failure. Parenteral nutrition carries significant risks (infection, metabolic complications) and is not indicated here.
(Choice E)
Start a high-calorie, high-fat oral nutritional supplement to increase BMI
While caloric adequacy is important in malnutrition, non-specific high-calorie supplements emphasizing fat and carbohydrates will not effectively reverse sarcopenia. Only protein intake stimulates muscle protein synthesis through activation of the mTOR pathway. In sarcopenic older adults, the quality and timing of protein intake matters more than total calories - leucine-rich protein sources are particularly effective at overcoming anabolic resistance.

pages.question: A 34-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician for preconception counseling. She and her husband have been trying to conceive for the past two months. She has no chronic medical conditions, takes no medications, and eats a varied diet that includes some fortified cereals and leafy vegetables. Her menstrual cycles are regular. She asks what specific dietary measure she should take now to reduce the risk of neural tube defects in a future pregnancy. Which of the following best describes the mechanism and recommended approach for neural tube defect prevention through dietary intervention?

answers.text:
Take iodine supplements beginning at conception to support fetal thyroid development and reduce the risk of neural tube defects
(0%)

Eat iron-fortified foods daily to prevent fetal spinal cord abnormalities associated with iron deficiency anemia
(0%)

Begin supplemental folic acid 400–800 mcg daily at least one month before conception to support one-carbon metabolism required for neural tube closure
(100%)

Consume omega-3 fatty acid supplements beginning in the first trimester to promote fetal brain development and prevent neural tube defects
(0%)

Increase dietary intake of vitamin A-rich foods to support fetal neurogenesis
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Folic acid, the synthetic form of folate, reduces the risk of neural tube defects by supporting one-carbon metabolism required for neural tube closure, which occurs between days 21–28 of gestation — often before a woman knows she is pregnant. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends 400–800 mcg of folic acid daily beginning at least one month before conception and continuing through the first trimester. Mandatory folic acid fortification of enriched grain products in the U.S. has significantly reduced the national prevalence of neural tube defects since 1998.
(Choice A)
Take iodine supplements beginning at conception to support fetal thyroid development and reduce the risk of neural tube defects
Iodine is critical for fetal thyroid hormone synthesis, and severe iodine deficiency during pregnancy can cause cretinism and neurodevelopmental abnormalities. However, iodine deficiency is not a recognized cause of neural tube defects, and iodine supplementation does not reduce neural tube defect risk. This is a distinct nutritional concern from folate-dependent neural tube closure.
(Choice B)
Eat iron-fortified foods daily to prevent fetal spinal cord abnormalities associated with iron deficiency anemia
Iron is essential during pregnancy to prevent maternal anemia and support fetal growth, but iron deficiency is not causally linked to neural tube defects. Neural tube defect prevention is specifically dependent on adequate folate, not iron. While iron supplementation is important in pregnancy, it addresses a different nutritional concern.
(Choice C)
Begin supplemental folic acid 400–800 mcg daily at least one month before conception to support one-carbon metabolism required for neural tube closure
Folic acid is the synthetic, bioavailable form of folate that participates in one-carbon metabolism, providing methyl groups essential for DNA synthesis and methylation reactions required for neural tube closure. Neural tube closure occurs between days 21–28 of gestation, a period during which many women do not yet know they are pregnant, making preconception supplementation critical. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends 400–800 mcg of folic acid daily for all women of childbearing age who are capable of becoming pregnant, beginning at least one month before conception. Folic acid fortification of enriched grain products was mandated in the United States in 1998 and has been associated with a 25–50% reduction in the incidence of neural tube defects nationally. Women with a prior pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect require higher doses of 4 mg/day under physician guidance. This is one of the most well-established examples of a fortified food policy producing measurable public health benefit.
(Choice D)
Consume omega-3 fatty acid supplements beginning in the first trimester to promote fetal brain development and prevent neural tube defects
Omega-3 fatty acids, particularly DHA, are important for fetal brain and retinal development and are recommended during pregnancy. However, they do not prevent neural tube defects, which are specifically prevented by adequate folate/folic acid intake. Additionally, starting omega-3 supplementation in the first trimester would be too late to prevent neural tube defects, as neural tube closure occurs by day 28 of gestation.
(Choice E)
Increase dietary intake of vitamin A-rich foods to support fetal neurogenesis
Vitamin A is important for fetal development, but excess preformed vitamin A (retinol) is actually teratogenic and can cause neural tube defects and other congenital anomalies when consumed at doses >10,000 IU daily. Increasing preformed vitamin A intake during preconception is not recommended for neural tube defect prevention and would be counterproductive and potentially harmful.

pages.question:

He denies jaundice, changes in stool color, or pruritus. Physical examination reveals mild epigastric tenderness but no palpable masses or hepatomegaly. Laboratory tests are shown below. What is the most appropriate next step in the evaluation of this patient?
